newsitem.title: POLAND: Demirel says Turkey will not block Poland in NATO.
newsitem.headline: Demirel says Turkey will not block Poland in NATO.

text.p: President Suleyman Demirel gave Turkey's assurance on Wednesday that his country would not block Poland's membership of NATO, and Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski declared himself fully satisfied.

Turkish officials including Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller in January appeared to suggest their country's parliament might not ratify the enlargement of NATO unless there was progress on Ankara's 10-year-old bid to join the European Union.
But after talks in Warsaw with Kwasniewski, who views fast NATO membership as a top Polish goal, Demirel challenged journalists to prove any such threats had been made.
"I repeat Poland will be a member of NATO and its biggest support will come from Turkey," he told a news conference.
Kwasniewski said he was satisfied Demirel was speaking for Turkey -- as he had made his comments before a Turkish delegation including members of all groups in parliament.
"I am convinced this is not just the standpoint of the Turkish head of state but of Turkey," Kwasniewski said.

Poland, which escaped Soviet domination only in 1989, hopes that NATO and Russia will later this month agree a document paving the way for new members to be invited, at the Western pact's July summit in Madrid, to start entry talks.
Poland expects to be among the first NATO candidates, along with the Czech Republic and Hungary.

The admission of new members, expected in 1999, must be ratified by parliaments of all 15 states in the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation including Turkey, so Kwasniewski hailed Demirel's assurances Ankara would not block Poland's path.

"I wish to recognise this declaration as very important, before the decisions which will be made at the end of May concerning the document between NATO and Russia and also the early july Madrid summit," he said.

European Union associate Turkey formally applied to join in 1987 but the European Commission has ruled that it is not ready on economic and democratic grounds. Other countries, including Poland, have seemed to overtake Turkey in the queue.
Demirel said Poland and Turkey both bridged East and West and both believed they would in future cooperate in NATO and the EU -- with its defence arm, the Western European Union.
Kwasniewski said he was sure Poland and Turkey would at some future stage both be in all European structures.
Demirel, who began a three-day official visit on Wednesday with a team including business leaders, oversaw with Kwasniewski the signing of an agreement designed to boost tourism.

They agreed on a need to boost trade, which registered turnover of about $150 million last year with a $35 million deficit for Poland, according to Polish figures. Demirel said they aimed to clinch an agreement freeing up trade in 1998.
They also aim to promote investment, with Poles developing Turkish power stations they helped build in the past, and Turkish entrepreneurs taking part in building Polish roads and infrastructure.
